introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Geography 2 (0550), Paper 2, ORDINARY LEVEL, JUNE 2024. Duration: Two and a Half Hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR Questions choosing ONE from each section.

Question ONE carries 30 marks. All the other Questions carry 20 marks each.

Each question that is sub-divided has the sub marks in brackets.

In questions involving calculations, all steps of the working MUST be shown.

If an outline MAP and/or GRAPH are used, they must be tied inside your answer booklet, opposite the written part of the answer.

NB - ONLY THE FIRST FOUR QUESTIONS ANSWERED WILL BE MARKED.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

questions.corrige_markdown:
**What is asked.** The candidate must draw a **sketch map** (a simplified copy of the map, not a tracing of every detail) of the part of the Dufftown extract that lies **north of northing 36 and east of easting 23**, **locate five features** on it, and add a **key** and a **scale**.

**Step 1 - The frame.** The part to be copied runs from easting 23 to the east edge of the extract (about easting 34) and from northing 36 to the north edge (northing 46). It is therefore about 11 km from west to east and 10 km from south to north. At the scale of the map (1:50 000, so 2 cm represent 1 km) the frame is 22 cm by 20 cm. A candidate may reduce it (for example to 11 cm by 10 cm, which is 1 cm to 1 km or 1:100 000), but then the scale on the sketch must be changed to match. Draw the frame, number the grid lines (eastings 23 to 34 along the top, northings 36 to 46 up the side) and draw only the few grid lines that help to place the features.

**Step 2 - Plot the five features** (distances measured from the south-west corner of the frame, easting 23 and northing 36, at 2 cm = 1 km; readings are approximate, to about 0.3 km).

| Feature | Position | From the corner | At 2 cm = 1 km | How to show it |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| (i) Hill at 291372 | easting 29.1, northing 37.2 (the hill named Meikle Conval, spot height 547 m on the map) | 6.1 km east, 1.2 km north | about 12.2 cm east, 2.4 cm north | a few closed contour rings with the spot height and the name, near the bottom of the sketch |
| (ii) Woodland | large block on the slopes of Blue Hill and the Dough of Edinvillie, roughly easting 28 to 30.5, northing 37.5 to 44; another block north of Archiestown, roughly easting 23 to 26, northing 45 to 46; small woods around Dufftown | - | - | outline the blocks and fill them with the woodland pattern or colour of the key |
| (iii) Road A941 | a main road coming from the Craigellachie area in the north and running south-east down the valley of the River Fiddich to Dufftown (about easting 32.5, northing 40) | - | - | a thick continuous line, labelled A941, following the bends of the road |
| (iv) Quarry at (3324407) | read as 332 407: easting 33.2, northing 40.7, on the north-east edge of Dufftown | 10.2 km east, 4.7 km north | about 20.4 cm east, 9.4 cm north | the quarry symbol of the map key, with its name |
| (v) Charlestown (of Aberlour) | built-up area beside the River Spey, about easting 26.8, northing 42.7 | 3.8 km east, 6.7 km north | about 7.6 cm east, 13.4 cm north | a small shaded or hatched built-up area with the name |

**Step 3 - Key.** Draw a box with one line per feature and use exactly the same symbols as on the sketch: *hill (contours and spot height); woodland (pattern or colour); main road (thick line); quarry (the map symbol); built-up area (town)*. Give the key a title.

**Step 4 - Scale and finishing.** Add a **linear scale** (for example a line 10 cm long, divided into 5 sections, labelled 0 to 5 km) and the **representative fraction 1:50 000** (or 1:100 000 if the sketch is reduced), a **north arrow**, and a **title** such as "Sketch map of part of the Dufftown area". Name the main features (Dufftown, Charlestown of Aberlour, Craigellachie, Ben Rinnes in the south-west) so that the sketch can be read without the original map.

**Marking guide (10 marks).** Frame, grid references and correct portion (2); each of the five features correctly located and labelled (5 x 1 = 5); key (1.5); scale and title / north arrow (1.5).

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) (i) Calculate the length of the road B9102
(ii) State the direction and bearing of Charlestown from Dufftown.

(4 + 3 = 7 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Length of the road B9102 (4 marks).**

The B9102 is the thick road marked with the red number B 9102 in the north of the extract. It leaves **Archiestown** (about easting 23.5, northing 44) towards the north-east, climbs past the label B 9102 (about easting 26.5, northing 45) and reaches the main road at the junction near **Craigellachie** (about easting 28.7, northing 45.3). The road continues west of Archiestown to the edge of the map, so the part measured here is the stretch **from Archiestown to the junction near Craigellachie**.

*Method.* A road is not straight, so a straight ruler is not used. Lay the edge of a strip of paper (or a piece of thread) along the road, marking its start, then pivot the strip at each bend and mark the end of every straight part, so that the whole length is transferred to the strip. Then measure the strip against the linear scale or with a ruler.

*Measurement:* the stretch measured about **11.4 cm** on the map.

*Scale:* 1:50 000 means that 1 cm on the map represents 50 000 cm = 500 m = 0.5 km on the ground (2 cm = 1 km, as printed in the key).

$$\text{Ground length} = 11.4\ \text{cm} \times 0.5\ \text{km per cm} = 5.7\ \text{km}$$

**The length of the B9102 from Archiestown to Craigellachie is about 5.7 km** (accept 5.5 km to 6 km, because the reading depends on the way the bends are followed). The straight-line distance between the two ends is a little shorter (about 5.4 km), which shows that the road is fairly direct here.

**(ii) Direction and bearing of Charlestown from Dufftown (3 marks).**

Dufftown is at about easting 32.6, northing 39.8 (built-up area at the east of the map) and Charlestown of Aberlour at about easting 26.8, northing 42.7.

- Charlestown is **to the west and a little north** of Dufftown: it lies **west-north-west (WNW)** of Dufftown (1 mark).
- *Bearing:* draw a straight line from Dufftown to Charlestown, draw a north line (a grid line) through Dufftown, and with a protractor measure the angle **clockwise from north** to the line. Check by calculation:

$$\Delta E = 26.8 - 32.6 = -5.8\ \text{km (west)},\qquad \Delta N = 42.7 - 39.8 = +2.9\ \text{km (north)}$$

$$\tan\theta = \frac{5.8}{2.9} = 2 \Rightarrow \theta \approx 63.4^\circ \text{ west of north}$$

$$\text{Bearing} = 360^\circ - 63.4^\circ \approx 297^\circ$$

**The bearing of Charlestown from Dufftown is about 297 degrees** (accept 290 to 305 degrees), written 297 degrees. The distance is about $\sqrt{5.8^2 + 2.9^2} \approx 6.5$ km, or about 13 cm on the map.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) (i) From map evidence only describe the site and situation of Dufftown.
(ii) Describe the distribution of road network and vegetation on the map.

(4 + 9 = 13 marks)

(Total 30 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Site and situation of Dufftown (4 marks).**

*Site* means the actual ground on which the town is built (2 marks). On the map, Dufftown (easting 32 to 33, northing 39 to 41, on the east edge of the extract) is a **compact built-up area on the lower, fairly gentle slopes of a valley floor** beside the streams (blue lines) of the River Fiddich and its tributary, where the contour lines are widely spaced and the ground is much flatter than on the hills to the west and south. The town is spread along the main roads, with its **buildings packed together** along the valley, and has a few farms and small woods round its edge. Slopes rise steeply to the west (Little Conval and Meikle Conval, with closely packed contours) and to the south-west (Ben Rinnes).

*Situation* means the position of the town in relation to its surroundings (2 marks). Dufftown lies **about 6.5 km south-east of Charlestown of Aberlour** and about 6 km south-south-east of Craigellachie, on the **eastern edge of hill country** (Ben Rinnes, Meikle Conval and Little Conval lie to the west and south-west). It is a **route centre**: the A941 from the Craigellachie and Spey area in the north-west reaches it, and other roads meet in the town from the south-west, the south and the east. It is also close to the Fiddich valley, which is a natural line of communication between the uplands and the River Spey.

**(ii) Distribution of the road network and of the vegetation (9 marks).**

**Road network (5 marks).**

1. **Main roads follow the valleys.** The main roads (thick lines) follow the **Spey valley** (the road along the river from the west edge through Charlestown of Aberlour to Craigellachie) and the **Fiddich valley** (the A941 linking Craigellachie to Dufftown). They avoid the steep, high ground.
2. **Roads converge on the towns.** Roads meet at **Dufftown, Craigellachie, Charlestown of Aberlour and Archiestown**, which are nodes of the network; Dufftown has the densest pattern of roads and streets.
3. **A high density of minor roads and tracks in the lowland farming areas**, for example the area between Archiestown and Charlestown and the Mortlach district north of Ben Rinnes, where many small roads and tracks link scattered farms (the names Mains, Easter, Wester and Upper on the map are farms and hamlets).
4. **Very few roads on the high ground.** Over **Ben Rinnes** (south-west), the Convals and Blue Hill, where the contour lines are close together, there are almost no roads, only a few tracks round the foot of the hills. Roads bend to go round the hills (for example the road south-west of Dufftown, which winds along the base of the Convals).
5. The **B9102** is a secondary road running north-east from Archiestown to the main road at Craigellachie. The pattern is therefore **dense in the valleys and near settlements, sparse on the uplands**, and roads are mostly roughly parallel to the rivers.

**Vegetation (4 marks).**

1. **Woodland (the "Wood" symbol of the key)** forms **large compact blocks on the hill slopes**: the long block on **Blue Hill and the Dough of Edinvillie** in the centre-east of the map and the block north of Archiestown in the north-west corner. Smaller strips and patches of woodland follow some river valleys and lie round farms and near Dufftown.
2. **The high ground of Ben Rinnes and the Convals** (south-west and south) is mostly **open**, with rough grazing, heath and rough grassland and **almost no trees** (steep slopes, thin soils, exposure).
3. **The lower, gently sloping land** (round Archiestown, Charlestown of Aberlour, the Mortlach district and Dufftown) is mainly **cultivated land and pasture** divided into **small fields**, with a few small woods and hedgerows between the fields.
4. A **moss (bog)** is named near the west of the map (about easting 22 to 23, northing 43), where the ground is wet and flat.

The vegetation is therefore **distributed according to relief and altitude**: farmland on the lowlands, large woods on the middle slopes and open moorland on the summits.
